URL: https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/pete-hegseth-resign-iran-joe-kasper-b3090554.html
The Independent, 24 Nov

Defense Secretary attacked over his leadership of the Pentagon by former aide Joe Kasper, who claims he has ‘lost any ability to be effective’ and is now a liability for the Trump administration

Pete Hegseth’s former chief of staff has called for the defense secretary to quit over his handling of the Pentagon and the Iran war.

Joe Kasper told Politico his old boss, who faces the threat of impeachment with the Democrats taking back control of Congress, has been “overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement”.

“Pete’s ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective,” the ex-aide said in a scathing interview, that also branded the Iran war a “s*** show”. “For that reason and others it’s time for Pete to call it quits.”

Kasper, who served with Hegseth for the first three months of his tenure last year, said he had been motivated to “speak truth to power” after the secretary was admonished for laughing and joking at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans’ Day.

The Air Force veteran said he felt Hegseth’s decision to award the guard who rebuked him at Arlington Cemetery a Joint Service Commendation Medal was an “attempt to trivialize” the humiliating moment, as “if that makes it all OK.”

He went on to accuse Hegseth of being “belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service” and said that the secretary’s refusal to engage in diplomatic niceties with lawmakers on Capitol Hill would come back to bite him, particularly after the Democrats’ triumph at the midterms led them to win control of Congress.

“He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill,” Kasper said. “He’s napalmed them… He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation.”

The former adviser said the secretary had engaged in “silly” culture war “distractions” and that he had realized early on in the job last year that it would be “all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it.”

“There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship,” Kasper said. “The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them ever less so now.”

He was also critical of Hegseth over the mass firings he has overseen at the Pentagon, removing some of the country’s top military leaders.

“These are real inspirational figureheads who were committed to the mission, but publicly they were treated in ways that would have made you think otherwise,” Kasper said, adding the Army had been left “essentially leaderless” and that “at almost every high-profile position, or every senior leader position, there’s a vacancy.”

“I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be,” he concluded.

Responding, a senior Pentagon official told Politico that the department was not surprised that a “disgruntled former staffer – someone who could barely survive 90 days in the building – is now peddling made up gossip to the media.”

“Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure,” the official said.

The Independent has also reached out to the Department of Defense for comment.

Hegseth was positive about Kasper when he left his role in April 2025, however, telling Fox News: “Joe is a great guy, great American. He has done a fantastic job for us at the Defense Department… You make changes over time, and we’re grateful for everything Joe’s done.”

Reacting to Politico’s interview during an appearance on CNN Monday, former Pentagon spokesman John Ullyot agreed with Kasper’s characterization of Hegseth as “ineffective,” saying he had been “an embarrassment” to President Donald Trump from early on and has since “inflicted real damage onto our military.”

Ullyot said of the Pentagon’s retaliatory attack on Kasper that it now had “a very inexperienced public affairs team” in place that would not engage with his criticism in a substantial way and were instead “attacking the messenger.”

“As soon as anyone becomes a critic… they try to attack them personally and it always falls flat,” he said, adding that he too thought Hegseth should step down, accusing him of telling the president what he wanted to hear on Iran, rather than the unvarnished truth.
